doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
title: What happened to the scores
summary: They discuss how arrangers left scores with leaders, how copies of The Song Is You survived, and Buddy Rich keeping the charts by his bed.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well I wouldn’t mind had having copies of a lot of things I did in those days, but in those days you never had copies, you wrote the original – that’s why music is so hard to find because the Xerox hadn’t been invented, there was no way to make a copy. And anybody that bought your stuff, owned it, so you gave them the scores and most of the time I never saw them 1111 again.
Would you believe I played with a band in D.C. fifteen years ago that had a copy of that chart.
Somebody that actually took a score to that chart?
No, as far as I know it was the original copied parts, I think somebody maybe had made a Xerox of the Joe Timer Band’s copy of it.
And as a matter of fact, I got this guy to give me a Xerox of the Xerox and then I gave it to my friend Bill Schremp so he’s got a copy of it. I played the chart.
I don’t know whatever happened to the score, I think all those guys got their copies right from the parts, somebody took them out of the books and copied them over night and brought them back.
I don’t think they ever took it off the score.
Although they could have ‘cause I always wrote transposed in those days.
Yeah the score is probably long gone.
Oh, I can’t imagine what happened to it.

‘Cause in those days it was common practice of course for arrangers when you wrote a chart for a band, you gave the leader the score and the copied parts and if you were lucky you got paid and that was the end of it.

Sure, yeah, you were lucky if you got paid. It reminds me of whatever happened to the score, when he was real sick, you know about the time just shortly before he died, Chauncey Welsch, he had played in the band, he wasn’t with me but he went to see Buddy and they were talking about all the old days and Chauncey said, “God, sure was nice playing those Johnny Mandel arrangements,” and Buddy says, “Sure was, I loved those,” and he says, “You got them, you still have them?” And Buddy says, “sure,” he points at the night table and says, “Right over there.”
